subject: paediatrics
title: Language Milestones and Early Social Skills

steps.tx: Early infant communication begins with smiling and responsive vocalization. A **social smile** appears reliably between six and eight weeks of age in response to a friendly human face or high-pitched voice, distinguishing true social interaction from spontaneous neonatal reflex smiling. Absence of a reciprocal social smile by three months represents an early red flag for visual impairment, maternal-infant attachment disruption, or broader developmental delay.
steps.say: A social smile emerges by six to eight weeks in response to human faces and voices. Spontaneous smiling occurs earlier during sleep, but reciprocal social engagement signifies neurological maturation. Failure to establish a reciprocal smile by three months indicates sensory deficits, maternal attachment failure, or developmental pathology.

vis.alt: Infant pulled from supine to sitting at four months, holding the head in line with the trunk without head lag.
vis.caption: Traction response in a four month old infant pulled to sit, showing no head lag as the head stays aligned with the trunk. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Postural control of the head precedes voluntary manipulative skills. Complete **neck holding** without head lag when pulled from supine to sitting should be established by four months of age. In the prone position, the infant lifts the head and upper trunk to ninety degrees supported on forearms by four months. Persistent head lag beyond four months warrants formal neuromuscular and developmental evaluation.
steps.say: Complete head control without lag when pulled to a sitting posture matures by four months. Prone head elevation to ninety degrees occurs concurrently. Persistent head lag at four months indicates hypotonia, congenital myopathy, or cerebral dysfunction.

steps.tx: Vocal sound production progresses from primitive vegetative phonation to structured linguistic expression. Pre-linguistic **cooing** consisting of musical vowel sounds such as ooh and aah emerges between two and three months of age during reciprocal face-to-face vocal play with caregivers. Laughing aloud emerges spontaneously by four months, reflecting positive affective arousal and auditory responsiveness.
steps.say: Cooing emerges between two and three months as open musical vowel sounds. Giggling and laughing out loud follow closely at four months. These pre-speech vocalizations require intact hearing and reciprocal social interactions.

left.title: Cooing Phase (2 to 4 Months)
points: Vowel phonation like ooh and aah
Accompanies social smiling and reciprocal vocal play with parents

right.title: Laughter Phase (4 to 6 Months)
points: Demonstrates affective pleasure and intact auditory feedback loops

steps.tx: Consonant-vowel repetition marks the transition toward articulatory motor control. Monosyllabic **babbling** with repetitive consonant sounds like ba, da, and ma appears at six months. Deaf infants may initiate brief cooing due to innate motor programmes but cease vocal play at six months because they lack auditory self-reinforcement, making persistent vocal silence at this age an urgent indication for audiometry.
steps.say: Monosyllabic babbling emerges at six months with distinct consonant vowel sounds. Hearing impaired infants may produce early cooing but typically fall silent at six months due to absent auditory reinforcement. Inability to babble at six months demands prompt audiological assessment.

rows: Single sounds like da and ba

steps.tx: Complex phonetic chaining allows production of repeated syllables. Bisyllabic vocalization, termed **canonical babbling**, appears around nine months of age with combinations like mama, dada, or baba used indiscriminately without specific reference to parents. The infant also imitates simple sounds like clicking tongues and responds consistently to maternal prohibitions such as saying no firmly.
steps.say: Canonical bisyllabic babbling develops at nine months, generating sequences like mama and dada without specific semantic meaning. The infant understands parental tone and responds to the word no by stopping actions momentarily.

left.title: Non-Specific Babbling (9 Months)
points: Repeats mama and baba randomly to any adult
Reflects motor articulatory skill rather than semantic comprehension

right.title: Specific Word Naming (12 Months)
points: Applies mama specifically to mother and dada to father

steps.tx: True symbolic speech emerges when acoustic signals consistently designate specific referents. Acquisition of the **first words** with clear intent occurs at twelve months of age, when the infant accurately addresses parents with specific mama and dada, alongside one or two additional single words. The one-year-old child also comprehends simple verbal commands paired with pointing or gestures.
steps.say: True words emerge at twelve months when mama and dada are assigned specifically to parents, plus one other distinct word. The child also executes simple one-step commands accompanied by pointing gestures.

steps.tx: Linguistic expansion accelerates dramatically during the second year of life. By eighteen months, a toddler typically commands an expressive vocabulary of ten to twenty words and points accurately to named common objects or pictures. The child also indicates physiological desires without crying, utilizing **pointing gestures** to share joint attention, which serves as a vital diagnostic exclusion for autism spectrum conditions.
steps.say: A vocabulary of ten to twenty words develops by eighteen months. The child points to desired items and demonstrates joint attention. Shared visual attention is an essential social communication milestone that excludes early autism.

left.title: Joint Attention Pointing (Proto-declarative)
points: Points at an aeroplane to show delight to parents

right.title: Instrumental Pointing (Proto-imperative)
points: Points merely to demand a biscuit or toy
May be retained even in social communication disorders

steps.tx: Combining distinct grammatical elements into meaningful phrases reflects syntactic maturation. The formation of **two-word phrases** containing a subject and verb, such as baby go or want milk, is achieved by twenty-four months alongside an expressive vocabulary exceeding fifty words. At this chronological age, roughly half of all spontaneous utterances should be readily understood by familiar family members.
steps.say: Forming two-word phrases containing a noun and verb emerges by twenty-four months with a fifty-word lexicon. Parents understand about half of the child speech at two years.
